utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. I know that there's one pending preliminary matter which is not of any urgence, so therefore I'd rather leave it. If the parties are ready, the witness could be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I address the Defence in relation to the 92 ter motion for Vojo Kupresanin. The Defence has tendered 38 associated exhibits for Witness Vojo Kupresanin, and the Chamber reminds the Defence that it prefers that documents are tendered through the witness in court and invites the Defence to reduce the number of associated exhibits. The two remaining issues are P6965 and P6926, revised translations. We'll deal with them but first wait for the witness to escort -- to be escorted in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Dobro jutro."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lelek. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic standing to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Could you please state your full name for purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Good morning. My name is Milovan Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would ask for 1D1765 in e-court. I had also prepared a clean paper copy that I gave to the Prosecution. I don't know whether they've had a chance to look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the monitor in front of you, first of all, can you tell us do you remember giving this statement to members of the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it, Mr. Ivetic, that you wanted the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, if the Prosecution has, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher assist in giving the statement to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my next question is: Looking at the first page of this statement, can you tell us whose signature we see on the cover page?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: This is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now turn to the last page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We see here a signature and a date. Can you tell us whose signature this is?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: This is also my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, subsequent to signing this statement earlier this year, did you have a chance to review the same in Serbian during proofing to verify if everything was correct in it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: During the proofing with the Defence team lawyers, I had an opportunity to review the statement and I realised that there were some things in there that needed to be changed because they do not reflect what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can first turn to page 3 in both languages, and I would like to look at paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in paragraph 12 there is a -- an associated exhibit that is identified as 1D03109, and did you and I ascertain that, in fact, the correct document that you are referring to is 1D03122?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can look at paragraph 13, the same page in Serbian, the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph there is a sentence that starts: "Two days after that, the Serb population and part of the Muslims evacuated ..." What can you tell us about the correct time-period that this sentence is applicable to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: This sentence should read instead of the "Muslims did not allow the body to be pulled out and thereafter a conflict with the Muslims ensued." This sentence should read after the sentence --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: This is impossible to interpret.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the interpreters have problems. Mr. Ivetic, perhaps you -- I take it that you're more or less aware and could you take it step by step so that the interpreters are able to provide us with the accurate translation of the changes the witness wishes to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And also focus on the same part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we can focus on the middle of the paragraph, you say: "Rogatica was completely liberated as late as 23 July 1992." And then the very next sentence starts: "Two days after that, the Serb population and part of the Muslims evacuated ..." To what time-period should the two days after that relate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: This should refer to the period after the 22nd of May, 1992, a day or two after the 22nd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could now focus on the last two sentences in this paragraph. To do so, we'll have to go to the next page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, if we could focus on the last two sentences. First of all, in -- the first starts: "After that, a decision was made that the town must be liberated ..." What you can you tell us about the placement of the last two sentences of this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The last sentence, "The civilian population was again safely evacuated, mostly Muslims," it should be moved and it should follow the sentence: "About 20 to 25 May, 1992, we were informed that long columns of civilians were on their way to Vragolovi." After that the sentence, "The civilian population was again safely evacuated, mostly Muslims," should be inserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in that sentence mentioning Vragolovi, you have a date listed as about 20 to 25 May and in the English it says 1995. In the Serbian it says 20 to 25 May 1992. Are either of those dates accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The accurate date is between 20 and 25 June.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Of what year?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we can turn to paragraph 14, which should be on the page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please clarify where now the -- after that decision was made that the town must be liberated from the armed Muslim forces. Where does this now find its place?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Judge is asking about the sentence that says: "After that a decision was made that the town must be liberated from the armed Muslim forces." How do we understand that sentence chronologically? Where does it fall, where does it belong?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That sentence should be the last in the paragraph, and it should follow the sentence which reads: "The civilian population was again safely evacuated, mostly Muslims." And after that, the following sentence should be inserted: "After that a decision was made that the town had to be liberated from the armed Muslim forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that was after the civilian population was safely evacuated. Could I also ask one -- already one short clarification. You said a decision was made. By whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command of our -- our brigade made that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And paragraph 14. Now, I'd like to focus on the last sentence which talks about the weapons that the Territorial Defence of Rogatica possessed, the military-issue weapons. Do you have any corrections to make as to what is recorded here?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I have a correction to make.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is reading too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, if you read, could you do it very slowly. Otherwise the interpreters are unable to translate your words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It says here that the Territorial Defence of Rogatica had possessed military-issue weapons for more than 500 soldiers. Before the war I worked in the Territorial Defence Staff and I know what the establishment of the Territorial Defence was at that time. I know that there were manoeuvre and special units. As for the manoeuvre unit, there was a staff with its units, there was the department of the Territorial Defence at the logistics base, and the reconnaissance units. Those manoeuvre units had a total of approximately 500 troops. There were also spatial units of the Territorial Defence which were the units of the local communes and companies. We had ten such units in local communes and 12 such units -- or perhaps 13 which were attached to various companies. There was a total of 1100 men in those territorial units in local communes and companies. There were also about 500 troops in the manoeuvre units. The grand total would have been 1500 troops and each of the soldiers had weapons issued to them. That's why I think that this is a mistake. Where it says that there were more than 500 soldiers, this figure should be replaced with the figure 1500 soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now let's look at paragraph 19 on page 5 in English and 5 in the Serbian as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in that paragraph -- in that paragraph, you discuss incidents involving aid convoys. Could you clarify for us which of these incidents were you personally present for?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: In paragraph 19 in the second sentence thereof, it says: "I remember that in the course of 1994 ammunition was found in a convoy transporting bags with flour." I personally participated when that convoy was stopped and controlled. I did not participate in the control of the convoy where sniper rifles were found. It was a Canadian convoy which was supposed to be transporting medical supplies. I wasn't there. But I did participate in the control of the convoy where ammunition was found instead of bags with flour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to look at paragraph 21 at the bottom of this page. So that we can have a proper translation of the first sentence, could you slowly read the Serbian to us, the first sentence of paragraph 21.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The biggest Muslim strongholds or the strongholds of Muslim forces were in the town centre at Ljun in the area of Zivaljevina in the villages of Ladjevina, Ferizovici, Pribosjevici, Stjenice, Brezje, Kladanj, Pokrivenik and Vragolovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what you can you tell us about all these villages that you have just read off? Do all of them belong in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: When I provided the statement to the Mladic Defence team, I stated that the biggest strongholds of Muslim forces were in the town centre at Ljun in the area of Zivaljevina, Pokrivenik, and Vragolovi. As for the villages of Ladjevina, Ferizovici, Pribosjevici, they had their observers there. Those were Serbian villages and from there we got messages about the movement of enemy forces, their strength, the location of those forces. From there, we received intelligence from our observers. I did not say that the strongholds of Muslim forces were in those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, apart from the corrections we've gone through today, do you stand by everything else in your statement as accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you questions today on the same topics as in your statements, would your answers to those questions be the same in substance as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: In substance they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And having taken the solemn declaration to tell the truth, would that mean that those answers, if you were to give them today, would be truthful?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D1765 as an exhibit. There are two associated exhibits that go along with it, 1D03122 and 1D04364.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic, I'm just seeking -- first of all, you said there was a translation issue and you invited the witness to read slowly. What was then interpreted for us was the same, I think, as what we saw in the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One word is missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One word is missing and that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Forces. There is a difference between a Muslim stronghold and Muslim forces stronghold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- yes. Muslim stronghold and the strongholds of Muslim forces. Yes. That's clear to me. Then as far as the associated exhibits are concerned, I'm just checking the numbers. Yes. Madam Registrar, the statement of the witness would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D01765 receives exhibit number D849, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D849 is admitted. Then the two associated exhibits. The first one, I think in the order as mentioned, 1D03122, would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D850, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 1D04364 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D851, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D851 is admitted. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I have the public summary that I'd like to read at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Milovan Lelek worked for ten years in the Rogatica municipal Territorial Defence until 1990. Thereafter, he worked as a teacher in the elementary school in Sljedovici village, until early March 1992 when Muslims set up roadblocks on the road leading to the village. Then with the situation in Rogatica becoming complex, he went to his parents' village of Dobromirovci and stayed there until the end of May. As early as March 1992, the Muslim population started leaving Rogatica and he saw on a daily basis armed groups of Muslims travelling from Rogatica towards Kopljevici and Pokrivnek. He found out about a Green Beret paramilitary commanded by Maher Muftic with a staff headquartered in one of Rogatica's mosques. Both mosques in Rogatica were destroyed during armed fighting when the town was under the control of Muslim forces. The witness went to Borike at the invitation of the Territorial Defence and joined the command there as a reserve captain first class. He recalls Radio Sarajevo reports misreported the situation in Rogatica to create a picture about wicked Serbs and victimised Muslims. He recalls incidents where humanitarian convoys were found to have ammunition in flour bags, sniper radios, and other military hardware. Helicopters were often seen flying towards Zepa and it was later learned these too carried military equipment. And that completes the summary of the evidence. I have a few additional questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, were there Muslim villages in Rogatica that stayed loyal to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: There were several villages in Rogatica that remained loyal to the Serb side: Zakomo, Berkovici, Burati, Satorovici, Okruglo, Strmac, Madjar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was the attitude of the Serb authorities in Rogatica to these villages that stayed loyal?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: The municipal civilian authorities regularly supplied these villages with everything they needed to meet their basic needs and also cattle feed, fuel, gasoline, crude oil, so that they could continue working in agriculture. Muslim loyal villages continued to live together with the neighbouring Serb villages, just as they did before the war. There was no difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what eventually happened to these loyal Muslim villages in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off while the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, we'll take the example of the village of Satorovici. They lived a normal life with the neighbouring Serb villages, and in that Muslim village General Asim Hodzic lived at the time as well. They were receiving regular supplies as I've already mentioned, and on one occasion on the road from Borike to Rogatica, in that village Radenko Bjelakovic and his daughter Sonja were ambushed and killed. Sonja's mother, his wife, survived, and these terrorists, if I can call them that, these Muslims who had ambushed them and who killed Radenko and Sonja told the mother, "Bitch, we're not going to touch you. We're going to leave you alive so that you could suffer for the rest of your life." The relations between the Serb and Muslim population remained good, so these inter-human relations were not disturbed to such an extent by this incident. But Asim Hodzic once personally asked that somebody come to his village because he noticed that near his village there were armed persons that were noticed, one or two, and then from the brigade command I think Commander Ranko Kusic went there, I can't remember who went from the municipality to talk to the general, and then the general asked to have the village searched to see whether somebody had planted some weapons there. Then in some shed some weapons were found, a hunting rifle and also a shorter rifle -- I don't know. And other things. Soon after that, probably because of all of these things that had happened, the general got sick and he asked to leave his village. We used our own car to take the general to the border with Serbia and from there he was taken to the military medical academy. The population stayed on there for a little while but they were afraid of Muslim extremists, they were afraid that they would be attacked again, and that armed groups would come in, again. They asked the Serb authorities, the civilian Serb authorities, they said that they wanted to leave their place of residence and they took buses --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we -- we do have some time limitations. I would ask if you could somehow briefly summarise whether the loyal ethnic Muslim villages that we discussed ended up staying in Rogatica or what happened to them. A little bit more briefer than this description of the one village.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, these villages did not stay in Rogatica for a long time. They were -- they asked our authorities for transportation. They wanted to leave. They were afraid that the Muslims would threaten them because they lived as good neighbours with the Serbs and they asked to leave these villages. That was made possible for them, and they went to places that were under the control of the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, thank you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I don't think that the answer responded to the question you have put. I thought you were asking about the Muslim population in these villages and not about the Serbs, who were then leaving. Please clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can have direction, Your Honours. I don't see where his answer talks about Serbs leaving. His answer talks about the Muslims leaving. Because they were good neighbours with the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see: "They wanted to leave. They were afraid that the Muslims would threaten them..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Because -- [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "... because they lived as good neighbours with the Serbs..."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. So it relates to the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Perhaps just so that we're clear, you've heard the Judge's inquiry, Mr. Lelek. Are you talking about the -- who are you talking about that was leaving from these loyal Muslim villages that were afraid that the -- that they would be attacked for being good neighbours with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, that goes for all the loyal Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And who -- what population within the loyal Muslim villages was leaving? What ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, of course they were Muslims. Muslims lived in Muslim villages. These were loyal villages. So it was Muslims who were living in these villages. But they were on good terms with the Serb villages that were nearby, that were near those Muslim villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, thank you for answering my questions. On behalf of my client General Mladic and the rest of the team, I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Before I invite the Prosecution to start its cross-examination, I have one question. Were those who had attacked General Hodzic and his daughter and killed his daughter, were the perpetrators found and arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. Then you misunderstood what I was saying. I did not say here that the general was attacked and killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I think my question was about the daughter having been killed. But then still, my question is: Were the perpetrators found and arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if you understand what I'm saying. I said that Muslim extremists on the road between Rogatica and Borike killed Radenko Bjelakovic and his daughter Sonja, and they -- and that they didn't want to kill her mother. They let her live so that she would suffer for the rest of her life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And my question is: What you said were Muslim extremists, were they caught, were they identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Never. They were never caught and no one knows who did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the Prosecution ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. MacDonald. You find Mr. MacDonald to your right. Mr. MacDonald is counsel for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, on the topic of this attack, you mentioned the name of a village. Can you repeat the name of that village slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I didn't understand you. What attack?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You spoke with the Presiding Judge about an attack that killed a father and daughter and left the mother alive. You mentioned the name of a village with that attack. It was not recorded on the transcript. Can you repeat the name of that village slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Satorovici is the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lelek, you testified as a witness in the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Karadzic Defence, and you were telling the truth when you gave that statement, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Under oath, just like now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And with regard to the statement you gave in this case, the Mladic case, you've had the opportunity to review it and make any corrections for the entire statement; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to have a quick look at your Karadzic statement, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31469 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be provided with a bit of ... could the glass be filled again. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to discuss the incorporation of the Rogatica Brigade into the VRS. Now, in your Karadzic statement at paragraph 15 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Which is page 4 in the English and page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, here in the first line, you state: "In May 1992, when the VRS was formed, the TO unit was reformed into the 1st Drina Light Infantry Brigade, and we used the shorter term, Rogatica Brigade, to referred to it." Now what you said there in your Karadzic statement, that's -- that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd now like to look at your Mladic statement, paragraph 14, page 4 in the English and 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is D849.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Now, just to repeat: Page 4 in both language, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In the first line here, you state: "After the VRS was established, the existing unit was transformed over time into the 1st Drina Light Brigade, which was called the Rogatica Brigade for short." The existing unit you refer to here, that's the Rogatica Serb TO, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: First it was the Territorial Defence, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And, sir, the words "in May 1992," which you gave in your Karadzic statement, don't appear in your Mladic statement. In fact, you've added that it was transformed over time. What's the reason for that change, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't see any change here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, you'd agree with me the words "in May 1992" don't appear, do they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I thought it wasn't necessary here for me to say May after the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska. And it is well-known that the army was established in May, and therefore I saw no need to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Very well. You're happy that your Mladic statement means that the TO unit, the Serb TO unit in Rogatica, became the Rogatica Brigade when the VRS was established?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Rogatica Brigade was subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in May 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: In May 1992, no, it wasn't under the Sarajevo Romanija Corps yet. And not the Main Staff of the VRS either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, your commander is Rajko Kusic; that's right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: He's reporting to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps by at least the 29th of May, 1992, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I know it wasn't at first, those first few days. When I arrived Borike, I know that the first report that I saw that was written was the 23rd of May, 1992. Because we sent that document to the commander of the TO of Sokolac and the Supreme Command of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We didn't sent it to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or the Main Staff. So I know at first in the beginning we didn't send those combat reports there, Territorial Defence. Not the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, not the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. I don't know exactly when it was that we started sending them to them. I mean, regular combat reports and other documents that are supposed to be sent to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P03907.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sir, this is an intelligence report from Rajko Kusic to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. It is dated 29th May 1992. If you can just read the date to whom it is being sent and who is sending it, you'll agree with me that's correct; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. Could he please be asked to speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please speak into the microphone and repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I cannot see this thing well. I mean, the letters are so small and then if I speak into the microphone, I cannot read what is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjust the microphone so that the problem will be resolved. And perhaps could it be even a bit enlarged, especially the upper part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. It can be seen here the 29th of May, 1992, a regular operations report sent to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, and what I claimed was that during the first few days when I arrived there, that reports were sent to the Territorial Defence, that we were not within the Sarajevo Romanija Corps or the Army of Republika Srpska. During the first few day, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: When exactly did you arrive in Borike, Mr. Lelek?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I arrived Borike - I cannot remember the exact date - but it was around the 18th, 19th, that's to say, the second half of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can direct your attention to the last line of the document in front of you, before it says Commander Rajko Kusic, he notes: "Problems, proposals, and requests - as in previous report." So it's clear that your commander has been reporting to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps even before the 29th of May; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I did not see those reports. I don't know what kind of reports these are. I'm just saying that I saw one on the 23rd of May that was submitted to the Territorial Defence of Sokolac. The 23rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'll ask my original question again then: Do you accept that the Rogatica Brigade was subordinated to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps by at least the 29th of May, 1992, having seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, according to this document, yes. According to this document, yes, but I cannot remember exactly when --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note: We did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your sentence. You said but you cannot remember exactly when, and would you then repeat what you then said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember the exact date when our brigade became part of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I see that this regular combat report was indeed sent to the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. I don't know whether our brigade was part of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I -- I fully understand that. But if you say I don't know whether our brigade was part of it at that time, may I remind you that in one of the previous answers you said it was not yet in May; where now, you say you do not know exactly. You know about the first days. And you accept that late May that they were. So you should be very precise in your answers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, you yourself were incorporated into the VRS on the 20th of May, 1992, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I was. On the 20th of May, I was in the Army of Republika Srpska. Actually, I was in the Territorial Defence, not the Army of Republika Srpska. The Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P06815.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is a list of officers from the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade being sent by Rajko Kusic to the Drina Corps Command. For the sake of clarity, the Rogatica Brigade was renamed to the Podrinje Brigade in August of 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You may not remember the date but you do know that at some point the Rogatica Brigade was renamed to the Podrinje Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we go to page 3 in both languages -- I wonder, Your Honours, if we might just use the B/C/S here. That's what we did when the document was admitted. It's simply the headings that have to be translated, and I'll ask the witness to confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, can you confirm you see your name appears second on this list?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And if we can move to the right, please. It's the ninth column, but we'll recognise it by the date, 25/1992. Yes, if we can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, you see a date, 20.05.92 --

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: What's the title of that column?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: "Date of Joining the VRS." But most probably that's what the form was like. There was no column that had date of joining the Territorial Defence printed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. Mr. Lelek, when you joined you became assistant commander for training and operations; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I became assistant Chief of Staff for education, not assistant commander. I was assistant Chief of Staff for training and operations. That was the exact title of my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. You say in your Mladic statement at paragraph 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I don't believe we need to call it up, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- that after you arrive in Borike that part of the command went to Rogatica, firstly to the Sladara facility. When did part of the command move?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date when that happened. Perhaps a month or two after I arrived they were moved to Sladara, but they came to Borike as well. But they spent most of the time in Sladara which was the new command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I have a few more questions on this topic, Your Honour. Probably finish in three or four minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's three or four minutes, I'll let you finish this topic and then we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Prior to the command moving, it remained in Borike; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: A part of the command. Borike was the forward command post. I was there as the assistant commander for training and operations, and there were two or three other officers who assisted me. Most of the command went to Rogatica, including the commander, the -- the chief of staff for training, operations, the chief of staff. They went to Rogatica and I remained in the forward command post in order to secure the area and prevent Muslim forces attacks from the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Prior to it moving, did your commander, Rajko Kusic, and the Chief of Staff, Mile Ujic, did they remain in Borike prior to the command moving to Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They were in Borike until the moment the command was moved to Rogatica. Obviously they were in Borika. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Rajko Kusic and Mile Ujic met General Ratko Mladic on the 30th of May, 1992, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, on the 30th of May, 1992, they're in Borike, you're in Borike, and you're an assistant chief in this brigade. How is it you don't know what your commander and the chief of staff are doing, particularly when they are meeting the commander of the entire VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I must have been on the defence line at that time. Perhaps I was not there. I was not at the command post. I was on the line where I inspected the troops who were there. And the brigade commander was not duty-bound to tell me everything. He had his chief of staff, and unless the entire command of the brigade had to be present, he did not have to tell me. I'm sure that whatever was discussed was not of such an importance that the whole command staff had to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This will be my last question before the break, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But your answers -- -- you say you didn't know. No one told you when you returned from the front line that General Mladic had visited the command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is: Whether no one, when you returned from the front line, told you that General Mladic had visited the command and had met with Kusic and his chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody told me that at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to enter the courtroom, I briefly deal with P6965 which was admitted on the 2nd of December through Witness Ratko Milojica, transcript page 29130. During the re-examination of the witness, the Defence raised an issue with the English translation of the document. On the 4th of December, the Prosecution did send an e-mail to the Chamber to advise that the revised English translation of P6965 had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0206-3526-ET, and that the Defence had indicated that it had no objection to it. Madam Registrar, you're hereby instructed to replace the current translation of P6965 with the revised one with the doc ID I just read out; that is, 0206-3526-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As always I take it that when the Prosecution reports that there are no objections by the Defence that there are no objections. If there be would, however, any problem, we'd like to hear within the next 48 hours. Mr. MacDonald, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Before I restart my questioning, Your Honours, just one matter from before the break. The basis of the question that General Mladic met with the chief of staff and deputy chief of staff comes from General Mladic's diary. There is no location recorded for that meeting, Your Honour. I just wanted to put that on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There are also two other documents referencing that General Mladic met with General Wahlgren and Colonel Wilson, that's P332 and 65 ter number 10624, so the Defence's position: It was not in Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Positions are clear. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, before I move on from this topic, you mentioned a report being sent by Rajko Kusic to the Sokolac TO and the Supreme Command of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 23rd of May, 1992. Do you know by the words "Supreme Command of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina" who Rajko Kusic was sending that report to?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: To the Supreme Command of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I think. I believe that it was sent to Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, finally, I'd like to look at your Mladic statement, D849.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I would like to go to page 3 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In your first line you describe reporting in late May 1992. You describe what you did until 1994. And in your last line, you state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Of which paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Paragraph 8, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In your last line, you state: "I know that in the initial period at that time we were in no manner connected to the corps or the VRS Main Staff." Given your evidence today, for the sake of clarity, that initial period must be no more than a few days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move to a different topic. If we can please have your Karadzic statement on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: That's 65 ter number 31469. And if I can have paragraph 13 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sir, paragraph 13 reads: "All this time we maintained courier, telephone, and radio contact with the main part of the command in Rogatica, and we sent daily combat reports on the developments in this area. At the beginning of 1994, I and the other officers with me in Borike were pulled back to Rogatica, where I was appointed Chief of Staff of the brigade." Now by the words "all this time," you're referring to a period from the end of May 1992 until your appointment as chief of staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And what you say here in your Karadzic statement, that's true, isn't it, you did have these communications?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: You mean with the brigade command in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I mean, sir -- or the question is: What I've just read you, that is true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: We, in Borike, could communicate with Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you also sent daily combat reports about developments in the area, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I'm not sure that it was daily, but we did send reports, especially on special events. If nothing happened on a particular day, on that day we did not send a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, sir, in your Karadzic statement it said you sent daily combat reports. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: If that's what I said, then it must be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: What I read to you from your Karadzic statement, the entirety of paragraph 13, none of that appears in your Mladic statement, sir. Is there any reason you did not mention these communications and these daily combat reports to the Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't think that there was a need for that. It's a well-known fact that combat reports were sent. We received combat reports from battalion commands. Then we amalgamated them into one report and sent that to our superior command. I did not think that it was necessary to emphasise that in my statement for the general.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: So your evidence is that it's a well-known fact that combat reports were sent. Is it equally a well-known fact that communications were working and that you had these communications?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the question. It's vague as stated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Communications with whom?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As well -- with ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well-known facts, Mr. MacDonald, are not the type of facts we are seeking, we are always seeking. So would be please be more concrete. Yes, I know that the witness said that it's a well-known fact, but I've heard many witnesses say what are well-known facts. Could you please try to focus specifically on what the witness can tell us. So would you rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, it isn't the case that you did not mention this paragraph because you knew you were testifying on behalf or in the case against General Mladic, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Object to the question. On the bases that: First of all, it misstates the witness's testimony and is not a restatement, as Your Honours had indicated of the previous question. It's unrelated to the previous question and it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I thought it was a new question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that Mr. MacDonald was putting to the witness. Mr. MacDonald, it was not a rephrasement. I mean, if you withdraw a question, that's -- Mr. MacDonald is entitled to do so and put a new question to the witness, so that objection is denied. Would you please put the same or another question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, to be clear, that's -- the last question it is where I am going with this line of questioning, as it were. So perhaps I can just put that to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then put it again to the witness because he may have forgotten what the question exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, is it the case that you did not mention the fact of daily combat reports and communications working within your brigade because you were aware that this case is against General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, not true. If this was not the General Mladic case, you would not put that question as well perhaps. Because this is a well-known fact --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is speaking too fast. It is impossible to interpret correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, Witness, you're talking too fast. We'll lose your words which we'd rather not do. So could you please resume from where you said: "Because this is a well-known fact ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to start his answer from the beginning because it was impossible to understand the gist of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're invited even to start the answer again on from the beginning. The question was about that you had not mentioned this because you gave a statement in the case against Mr. Mladic. Would you please start your answer again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as this question is concerned, it is not correct that I omitted the question. I did not omit it. Especially not because I'm testifying in the Mladic case, because I thought that that question was a well-known question. It is a well-known fact that regular combat reports are sent by the battalion commands to the brigade command, and that then the brigade command sends its regular combat reports to the superior command which is the corps command. That's why I did not feel the need to highlight this question in my statement, not only because it was the General Mladic case. Even if a case was against some other general or colonel, I would still not mention this question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So there's no change whatsoever so that daily reports were sent and communications were functioning, although you didn't think it important to mention it again. Is that the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we move to paragraph 15 of the statement. I think I need page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to read you a sentence, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In B/C/S, I believe it begins with the word "naoruzani" and in English it is six lines from the bottom, beginning: "We were armed ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It reads: "We were armed with weapons of the former Rogatica TO that had until then been kept in the JNA depots in Uzamnica and Visegrad." And it's true that you were armed with weapons that were previously in the JNA depots in Uzamnica and Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This has been referenced as the Karadzic statement. However, I just now realised that the translation that's being used is not the official translation, it's a draft translation, not the one that was introduced into evidence which I see and hold in my hand is a CLSS translation and which has different page numbers. So I just wanted to make clear that the document that's being used by the Prosecution is not the Karadzic statement that was introduced into evidence in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now let me just ... paragraph 15 of this statement. Which statement were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The Karadzic statement, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Karadzic statement. Yes. Which is on the screen. And, Mr. Ivetic, you said it's the wrong translation used or?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I see on the screen it says "draft translation." The official translation done by CLSS is page 3 and this is page 4, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But which one was admitted in the Karadzic case, the official translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This one. That's what I'm holding in my hand. It's in e-court as 1D04363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, I do not know where you found this translation and why you used that rather than the one which was admitted in the Karadzic case, but I don't know how important and how relevant the differences in translation are, but ... Do you have the -- the one, Mr. Ivetic is referring to? That translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I am certain it can be called up, Your Honours. I had understood this one to be the one in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But apparently it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: But apparently it's not. I wonder if we could call up in e-court that I missed there or my friend has referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that can be shown on the screen, then we can move on. And if it's -- is it just page numbering or is there any difference in the translation, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to look at the translations in detail to compare the two, but I know this the one that was introduced into evidence and this is -- and is indeed that we put in e-court. It should on page 3 in the English that this paragraph is located.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is paragraph 15, I do understand. Mr. MacDonald, you have prepared your questions so I take it that in your glance you could -- would be able to see whether anything there's which --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would bother you having used a different translation while preparing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: It is the same certainly in English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then please move on --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- with this -- with your questions in relation to paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm going to read you out this sentence, Mr. Lelek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: As I said previously, in the B/C/S I believe it's the line beginning "naoruzani."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it reads: "We were armed with weapons of the former Rogatica TO that had until then been kept in the JNA depots in Uzamnica and Visegrad." And my question is: It's true that you were armed with weapons that had been kept previously in those JNA depots, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: It is not construct in Uzamnica and Visegrad. What is correct -- what is correct is Visegrad. Here it says Uzamnica near Visegrad. So these are two different things. It is not Uzamnica and Visegrad but Uzamnica is close to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Okay. So there's a JNA depot at Uzamnica which is near Visegrad. Again, were you armed with weapons of the former Rogatica TO that had until then been kept in that depot?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, in the next line, you say you're unaware that the JNA armed Serbs in Rogatica. If we could have your Mladic statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Which is D849, at -- I would look for paragraph 14, which is page 4 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The last line in this paragraph is similar, that you were unaware that the JNA armed the Serbs in Rogatica. However, the part about being armed with weapons that had until then been kept in a JNA depot does not appear. Why did you not mention that to the Mladic Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I made a mistake by omitting it. It's just an error because I said everything else here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The witness is reading very fast. We don't know from where.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, again, you should slow down, especially when you're reading. You said it was an error because everything else here, and then you started reading what is in the document which also appears in the Mladic statement. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is written here is that I do not know that the JNA armed Serbs in Rogatica, because our pre-war Territorial Defence of Rogatica had standard-issue weapons for over 500 -- actually, 1500 persons. So the only thing I omitted here is that these weapons of ours were kept in Uzamnica near Visegrad. That's the only thing that I omitted to mention. Everything else is there and everything else is correct except for Uzamnica near Visegrad. So I just made an error in not mentioning Uzamnica near Visegrad, that our weapons were kept there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's a little bit more. But could I ask you a few questions about that statement taking. The text, indeed, if I quickly look at it from your Karadzic statement and the Mladic statement, is almost literally the same. You said you made a mistake when you did not mention this specific -- the JNA depots. Did you work on the basis of your Karadzic statement when you were interviewed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That statement was mentioned to me. I tried to say everything I said there over here as well, but then this error slipped in, that I didn't mention Uzamnica near Visegrad, and it is well-known that in 1991 when the army came and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you are going beyond what I asked you. Now you said -- does it mean that you gave that statement spontaneously when it was mentioned, or was it shown to you, that old statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, no, I had the statement. I had the statement and I read it several times. After the lawyers -- or rather, before the lawyers from General Ratko Mladic's Defence came, and I tried to avoid any differences between the two but then things slip in. But I really don't see that there's any problem here. I mean, that I didn't mention Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't have to worry about whether there are any problems. Earlier you said when we were talking about the daily reports that you considered it not of such importance that you should repeat it where it was commonly known that daily reports were sent. Now, there again we see that the two statements are very similar in language but there is a difference. Now, who then decided that it was not important to repeat that? Did you do that or was this suggested by those who interviewed you, that it was not important? Could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I decided that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You decided that. Was it your own idea that it was not important? You suggested that and then decided that, or was it suggested to you and that you then decided to leave it out?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have trouble hearing the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you re-start your answer and talk more slowly so that the interpreters can tell us your words.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all other microphones be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thought - and that's what I suggested - that it wasn't really that important to have this included in the statement, the sending of combat reports, because I thought that this was well known, that combat reports are being sent, so that that was not necessary. As for this thing here, Uzamnica, I forgot to mention that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness -- well, apparently you were working on the basis of the old statement, and then you made a suggestion that -- that portion about the daily reports could be left out because you considered it not to be important. That was your own suggestion. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, apparently you have thought over quite carefully what was needed to be repeated and what was not needed to be repeated. Now, in relation to the JNA depots from where the TO received -- the depots kept by the JNA, was that similarly that you thought that there was no need to tell that, or was it suggested to you or is it just -- just a mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a mistake. I forgot to mention this place, Uzamnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you worked on the basis of the old statement. The remainder of that paragraph is literally the same - almost literally the same, I should say - as we find it in the old statement. If you're working like that, does that mean that you repeated every sentence of that old statement and that it was then recorded again as what you said then, or did you go through it and say, This should be changed, that is relevant, this is not relevant? Could you explain to us a bit more in detail how that worked and specifically on the part you said you'd forgotten.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We worked on the basis of the old statement, and I made an effort to say everything I said in President Karadzic's statement, because I spoke under oath then as well. I wanted it to be similar to the statement I'm giving to General Mladic. So everything is the same here expect for Uzamnica, that was not mentioned. That was an error. When I spoke for this statement to be written up, I simply forgot this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now no one told you, since we're working on the basis of the old statement, haven't you forgotten something? Because there's a line in the old statement which you didn't repeat. Did no one bring this to your attention, that just a line was missing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody. They probably didn't notice it then either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we move to paragraph 19 in the Karadzic statement, please, which I think is the next page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Paragraph 19, Mr. Court Officer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see any of this. Can it be enlarged a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The beginning of paragraph 19 or the end? Because it's not identical at the moment on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and that's my fault. Sorry. It should be the beginning of paragraph 19, so the previous page in the English, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, the first line here reads: "I knew that there was a military detention facility was in Rasadnik." Now what you've said here in your Karadzic statement, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can move to the Mladic statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's paragraph 17 which I think is page 5 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The first line here, sir, reads: "I am aware that a detention facility existed at Rasadnik ..." Now the word "military" has been removed here, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to see where the word "military" arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's in the Karadzic statement? Could we have that -- we just had it but it's not visible at this moment. Could you repeat the number so that I can -- because we, of course, can consult it also on our own system. Could you repeat the number, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, the number of the Karadzic statement is 1D04363.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And it's paragraph 19, the first line, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we have a look at it because my legal page is not on my computer at this moment, so I have some difficulties in having access to it, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And one page back in the English. It is the first line of paragraph 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you see it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The description is military detention facility or detention facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct. I was looking at the English of the -- what I thought was the Karadzic but was actually the Mladic that was on the screen, so I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- mistaken between the two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think there is no translation issue here. I see the word "vojni" in the B/C/S first sentence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If we can go back to the Mladic statement, that's D849, page 5 in the English, page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You may put your question because everybody has seen it and the witness has the hard copy in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, the word "military" which appears in the Karadzic statement has been taken out of the Mladic statement, hasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That's right. The word "military" is not there. But further down you can see that soldiers were being detained. It even says soldiers of Serb ethnicity. So I believe that this is an error. Since there's a war going on, of course it's military. I cannot see what the issue is. Could you just enlarge this a bit up here because I cannot see it properly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've answered the question. Mr. MacDonald will now put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And we are, at the moment, not on the Mladic statement but the Karadzic statement again. But I think you should move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, I'm going to put to you that in fact these changes or omissions to your Mladic statement are an effort to minimise the involvement of the VRS and the accused in this case in the events in the municipality of Rogatica. Do you have any comment on that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That is not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll turn to the topic of Rasadnik and the situation there. In your statement you say you visited Rasadnik and you saw some people there; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You gave an interview to the police in Rogatica on the 17th of June, 2004; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I cannot remember the exact date. Could I have that document here now, if you have it? I don't have the exact date when it was that I was interviewed. Could I have that document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have 65 ter number 31403.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, this is a record of that interview, Mr. Lelek. I'm going to read a part out for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: In the B/C/S, it begins in the middle of the paragraph just after the letters BPC. In the English, it is at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can intervene, I note that the -- my learned friend is being misled by the incorrect translation of the title of the document which is, in B/C/S, "Sluzbena Zabiljeska," "Official Note" not "Official Record."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to my friend for his clarification, although I don't think it will affect my cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed. And take care that the right translation will be uploaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, the sentence reads: "He also did not know anything about the activities of establishing collection centres in the territory of the municipality of Rogatica (Sladara, Rasadnik, Parohijski Dom, elementary school and secondary school) before he came to Borike in 1992 where the FCP (forward command post) of the Rogatica Brigade was located in the hotel. He heard from some persons he did not know that there were collection centres in the town area, in the above-mentioned facilities, where citizens of Bosniak nationality were kept and from where they were later transported by buses to the territory under the Army of BiH control. "He also said that did he not know that the persons in the collection centres were mistreated or tortured in any way. During the time the above-mentioned centres existed, he did not come into the areas where they were located." Mr. Lelek, was that the truth that you told the police, that you did not come into the areas where these centres, which include Rasadnik, were located?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I see the date here when I gave this statement. It wasn't a statement. It was an Official Note by an official at the Ministry of Interior. The duration of this short statement that I gave to him, he asked four or five questions, he asked me whether I knew when the Crisis Staffs were established and I said I don't know, then he asked me: Do you know that there were collection centres, and then I said I heard about that when I arrived in Borike. Then do you know about these supplies, and I said, no, I never entered these facilities. So when he asked me whether I knew there was torture, whether people at the collection centres were being abused, and I said I don't know, I never entered these facilities. This went on for four or five minutes. He compiled an Official Note. Beforehand, I never had an opportunity to read this until the trial of President Radovan Karadzic. And everything that is written here is not the way I had said it. He added --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, again the interpreters are unable to hear you. So would you please slowly conclude your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this employee of the Ministry of Interior, from Rogatica, asked me whether I knew that there were some torture over persons who were in collection centres, I said that I did not know because I did not enter these facilities, these centres. I see that what he wrote here is that I had stated that I did not go to the area of these locations. Let me tell you one more thing. You see here that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, wait for the next question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But then -- Mr. Orie, it has to do with this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I have to clarify why this note is not meritorious for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The only question that was put to you is whether, in the relation to specifically entering those facilities, whether you told them the truth or not. And I think you've told us now two or three times that when asked about awareness of persons being tortured there, that you were not aware because you never entered those facilities. And in that respect, you've answered the question. Mr. MacDonald will now put his next question to you. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd like to move onto the substance of Rasadnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, before we do so, you said several times that you did not -- that you told them that you had not entered these facilities, whereas in your statement we read that you visited persons detained in Rasadnik several times. There seems to be a contradiction. Do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not enter those facilities, but I did come to the location of these facilities; that is to say, I came to Rasadnik where the military detention facility was but I did not go in. If I needed one of our soldiers who had escaped from the front line or who had done something, I asked the security detail there to get that soldier out for me, but I did not enter the detention facility itself. Also the collection centres, I never entered them in Rasadnik or in the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just then for my understanding, those who were detained there and you wanted to interview, they were taken out, outside the building, and then you interviewed them in the open air or -- I'm just trying to understand exactly what it is that you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For example, if NN left the front line arbitrarily and I know that is he in the military remand prison, I would get there and I would ask the guard, Get NN to come out in front of the prison. And there was a table there, and I sat there and I talked to him about what it was that I wanted to talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did they also bring the Muslims you saw there out of the building and to be seated at that table? Because you say that, I also saw some Muslims whom I knew from before, talking about Rasadnik. Were they also taken out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went there, I saw two or three Muslims that I knew walking around. I, however, spoke to the Serbian soldier. I never spoke to any of the Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I do understand that this was a detention facility. Were the Muslim detainees walking freely outside of the building? I'm just trying to get a picture of what exactly was the situation when you saw these Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can give you an example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went there to hold that conversation with a -- go ahead. I don't know what I need to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if -- if the example you are giving me is an answer to my question, you are invited to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is an answer to your question. When I went there to interview one of our soldiers who had left the defence line, while I was sitting there, very close to me, some 5, 6, metres away from me, Sefik Murko was passing by. He had been captured and he was in that detention area. He passed by me, I saw him, I knew him from before. I called his name, he approached me.
