I asked him if he needed something, and then he said, Mico, that was my nickname, do you have cigarettes. I would like to light a cigarette. And I would like to ask you, my mother has already left together with the other civilians. Can you help my father as well. I told him I'll do whatever I can. You just talk to me. That was the conversation I held. He was just strolling around the detention facility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, a minute ago you said: "I never spoke to any of the Muslim soldiers." And now you are telling us that you spoke to this specific Muslim, Sefik Malko. Which one is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that I did not investigate any of them because that was not my duty. I did not try to find out why they were in prison, why they had been captured. I knew this particular person. I called his name, and I gave him cigarettes. I just treated him to cigarettes. That's all. He was my neighbour. I knew him from before. In my previous answer, I meant any of the Muslim soldiers who needed to be interviewed and investigated. That was not my duty. That's why I never talked to any of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But this is not what you said. You said, I never spoke to a Muslim soldier. I leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I see we have one minute until the break, Your Honour. I don't know if you wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what you are able to perform in one minute, but if you think it's better to wait until after the break, then we'll follow your suggestion. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes; quarter past 12.00. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any time indication, Mr. MacDonald?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I would estimate between 20 and 30 minutes, Your Honours. Hopefully 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you stay within your time-limits. We'll resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I think that we had P6926 as a leftover. New translation as well? I ... Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We have received a revised English translation for 6926. I can address that now quickly on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you do it quickly, then...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As the Court will recall, that document was admitted through Witness Sarenac on 18th November 2014, and that can be found at T 28514 through -17. A translation error was brought to our attention, and you can see that reflected in 28544 through -45, on the 19th of November, 2014. So the revised translation has been uploaded into the e-court. It can be found under doc ID 0202-9875-ET. Assuming that if -- we have not spoken with the Defence about this yet, but if they have no objection to the revised translation, we would request that the Court Officer be instructed to replace the current translation with it. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We usually give an opportunity to revisit the matter within 48 hours. Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the English declaration attached to P6926 by a new translation which is known under number 0202-9875-ET.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, Muslim civilians who had not committed any crimes were detained in Rasadnik, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, they were not. The civilians who had not committed crimes were not detained. They were just accommodated there. They were not kept there in detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P06804.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, this is a list from the Drina Corps Command dated 1st of February, 1993. You'll see in the line above the list that the Drina Corps command are describing these people as prisoners. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should say "prisoners of war."

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution does not accept they're prisoner of war, but it was the prisoners that I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, but, if you put a document to a witness, you can't say, I disagree with part of that and therefore I read only part of that. Mr. MacDonald, you are drawing the attention of the witness to what is found in this document, and then you should read it in its entirety. Witness, could you please answer the question, whether you see that the persons on this list are referred to as prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that that's what it says here. But this is perhaps because of the exchange. Civilians could not be exchanged. Civilians could go of their own free will to the territory under the control of the BiH Army. This is most probably due to the fact that they needed to be exchanged. That's why they were referred to as prisoners of war. These were people were not prisoners of war. I can see that there were civilians among them. I'm sure this is about some exchange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, where do you see the word "exchange" in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's my assumption because the civilians who were here have been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. You're not being asked about assumptions. You're being asked about facts on this document, okay? You're not asked to interpret the document. You're asked to see what the document says. I'm done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can you take to number 4, Hanua Kustura. The date of birth recorded here is 1892. So she would have been 101 at the time this list was made; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And you'll see her address as recorded as Jasenica next to year of birth?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P06085S -- 6805, my apologies. 6085 -- 6805, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is a Drina Corps command sending a list to the Eastern Bosnian command dated 10th of April, 1993. And, at number 4, we see someone recorded as Hanuma Kustura but with date of birth 1892 and the village given as Jasenica, don't we?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And this time this list is being described as a list of captured persons of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I still claim that this list contains a lot of civilians. They had not been captured. My assumption is that there was going to be an exchange which is why they included civilians into the list. I claim with full responsibility that this Hanuma Kustura was a civilian who was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think in view of the age there could hardly be a lot of dispute about this to be not a soldier. But assumptions is not what we are seeking. If you have any knowledge -- and what Mr. MacDonald has done is to put to you a list dated the 1st of February, 1993, and then another list, 10th of April, so apparently no exchange had taken place. If that would be the explanation, the person still was there, five, six weeks later. Please proceed. At least as recorded in this document. And that's what Mr. MacDonald, I think, wants to bring to your attention. Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we please now move to P06722.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: This is a report on a prisoner exchange from October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I'd look for page 3 in the B/C/S, page 4 in the English. And I'm looking for number 11 on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I'm correct that this report states: "According to the Serbian side, she died at the age of 101 while in Rogatica-Rasadnik prison?"

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know who drafted this report. It is possible that she died in June in the reception centre. She did not die in prison. It is quite possible that she died, she was 101 years old, but she probably died in the reception centre, not in -- in prison. There were cases of people of Serbian ethnicity who were dying of old age as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, first of all, you were not asked about any persons of Serbian ethnicity. Do you have any specific knowledge that she died anywhere else than in Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no other knowledge. The only thing I claim is this: If she died, she died in the reception centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you have no knowledge about it, you told us, unless you mean to refer to Rasadnik as a reception centre. Is that what you are telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rasadnik was both a detention centre and a reception centre. It was reception centre for civilians and elderly people, and it was a detention centre for soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you do not know where she died. And none of the documents is talking about a reception centre, but all the documents shown to you are talking about prisoners and about prison. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who drafted this document. This is my comment. Nobody from our command drafted this document. I'm sure. And nobody from our command would have called this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The authors of the documents did. Please proceed, Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can we now move to P06806.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lelek, this is an exhumation report from the municipality of Rogatica carried out by the cantonal court of Sarajevo dated 4 November 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'd look for page 9 in the English, page 7 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And the name at number 11, Hanka Kustura. The heading of this section, sir, is "Rasadnik (Rogatica)." Now, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the last time this document was used, and I believe it was Ms. Bibles who was using it, you invited that I could check the co-ordinates on Google. I did. The co-ordinates that I came up with in Google by plugging in these numbers do not arrive in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, there was discussion on this document. You can find it at T-26414 to 26416. And I believe Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, requested the Prosecution to discover if there had been an autopsy. We have not found an autopsy report on this -- on this person, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any comment on the co-ordinates which put this person, perhaps other persons as well, I've not looked at it yet, outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I have no -- no comment upon that at the moment, Your Honours. I haven't checked that personally, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: The other piece of information that I wish to bring to Your Honour's attention is that my colleague misspoke in saying she was found in a mass grave. The transcript testimony is -- I provided -- in fact, it is a single grave although amongst other single graves in the same area. That is the extent of the information we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, there seems to be dispute about the area which may need to be further explored. What explains that you found this to be outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Are we using different grid references.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or is these the correct grid references? Is it military maps? Is it -- is it on the basis of the -- the global -- how do you call that? What the satellites tell us. Yes, the locations --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: GPS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, GPS gives us a kind of positions. This is X 38, Y 59. Well, we have to -- east and north. Let's have a closer look at it. That does not prevent you from putting questions at this moment to the witness on it, but it certainly needs to be further explored.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honours. And I only rose because I had had discussions with Ms. Bibles, and Mr. MacDonald is correct as to the other elements that Ms. Bibles had advised me of that she had confirmed, and those are the items that have been raised. And so we wanted to just make sure that was clear now that we have this document before us again. But obviously, they're allowed to ask questions about the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, I'm going to put you to that on the basis of what happened to Hanka Kustura, Rasadnik prison was used to detain Muslim civilians, including elderly women, who were then meant to be used for exchange. It was not a reception or collection centre. Isn't that the case, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, it is not. It was a reception centre for civilians, and it was a detention unit for prisoners of war. This lady, Hanka whatever her name is, Kustura, she may have died in Rasadnik, but she did not die in the detention unit. She died in the rooms which -- where civilian -- civilians were accommodated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, how do you know that, where she died?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've just said that she died in Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I didn't say anything. I asked you how do you know where she died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor told me that she died in Rasadnik, and I claim if she died in Rasadnik she died in the reception centre not in the detention unit because Rasadnik was split into two: There was a reception centre and there was a detention facility --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter missed the last bit of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard that several times. I just wanted to know how do you know where this person died.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know because they were not kept in the detention unit. They were not prisoners of war. That's how I know. I know that she was in the reception centre. That's how I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How do you know that this person was not in the Rasadnik prison? How do you know that? Have you ever met her? Have you seen her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never met or saw her, but when I went to Rasadnik because of our fighters, I was told where the reception centre was and where the detention unit was. I never saw that woman. I didn't know her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That was just speculation. It was not a fact you testified about; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I claim that 101-year-old woman was not kept in the prison but she was kept in the detention unit -- or rather, she was kept in the reception centre, not in the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. You are claiming that but you have no facts. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I'll move to my final topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: -- Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, I'd like to speak to you briefly about Muslims leaving Rogatica municipality. Muslims were forcibly transferred out of Rogatica municipality in, amongst other times, August 1992, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You are aware that Radislav Ljubinac was found guilty, amongst other things, of forcibly transferring women and children out of the village of Seljani -- sorry, Muslim women and children out of the village of Seljani and Rogatica municipality to Sarajevo in August of 1992, and he was found guilty by a court in Bosnia. You are aware of that, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I know that Radislav Ljubinac was found guilty and sentenced, but I don't know why. I never asked him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the first name of this person, Radislav or Radoljub?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Radislav, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Radislav Ljubinac was a member of the Rogatica Brigade, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If I can move to October 1994. And Muslims were forcibly transferred out of villages in Rogatica municipality then as well, weren't they.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, they were not. All the villagers volunteered to leave their place of residence. They did it of their own will. Nobody forced them to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have P06830. This is an article from the "New York Times" on 6 October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I just wonder if you can read the first four paragraphs for me, just to yourself, and let me know when you've finished reading, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I can't say anything. I've not seen this document before. I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Well, sir, I believe earlier today when my friend asked you about loyal Muslim villages, you mentioned the villages of Burati and Satorovici. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And there are two people here who are stating they were told to leave: The one from Burati by Serbian soldiers; and the one from Satorovici by the Serbian authorities. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: These villagers that were loyal, they were first taken to the collection centre in Rogatica, and it was their own wish to go to Sarajevo, I don't know, Kiseljak, wherever people wanted to go. And then when there was a larger number of them, buses took them to areas that were under BH Army control.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You didn't speak to these people leaving personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You don't know if they were leaving voluntarily, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I know of several cases. I know the village of Zahum that was loyal. I know that they called Radivoje Planojevic, who was their neighbour, and asked him to call the Municipal Assembly of Rogatica to have transportation provided for them because they couldn't take it anymore because the Muslim village of Uskoplje was threatening them. They said that they would kill them because they were co-operating with the Serbs. So they asked Planojevic for a bus, and Planojevic called the president of the municipality, they sent a bus to their village, and they boarded the business, and they were taken to the collection centre in Rogatica, and from there they went further on. So they asked voluntarily asked to have transportation provided for them so that they could leave. They no longer dared to live in their own village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: You didn't speak personally to any of the people leaving from that village, did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: No, no one personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And this report that we read in front of us is quite clear that people were forced to leave from the two villages named; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know to whom they gave statements and under what conditions. I know exactly how things went in these loyal villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Can the Prosecution please have back on the screen P06722.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, this is the document concerning the exchange of prisoners that noted that Hanka Kustura had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: And I would ask for page 4 in both languages. It's at the top in the B/C/S and it is just underneath the list that I am looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just going to read to you this paragraph and then ask you for your comment. It -- the author writes: "Unfortunately, I have to write that the Karadzic Serbs have taken advantage of the 1 October 1994 agreement signed at the airport in an attempt to use the prisoner exchange as a means of legalizing actions which carry all the traits of the crime of genocide. In that sense prior to the exchange the Karadzic Serbs had, on 5 October, expelled the remaining Bosniak population from four Rogatica villages: 66 women, children, and elderly in total. On 10 October, they expelled another 21 residents of the villages of Burati and Kovanja, leaving these territories purely Serb inhabited." Mr. Lelek, it is true, is it not, that the Bosnian Serb authorities used prisoner exchanges as an opportunity to further ethnically cleanse Rogatica municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That's not true either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. MacDonald. Before we give an opportunity to re-examine the witness, I would have a few questions for the witness. Witness, you explained to us several times that the persons in the reception centre had to be made prisoners of war in order to be able to be part of an exchange. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand it correctly. When I saw that list of prisoners of war, I thought that maybe somebody had asked from the Muslim side for prisoners of war so that they could be exchanged and that that is why they put civilians on these lists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I'm just trying to understand, if you would have left those elderly civilians to go there -- where they wanted to go, why would the other side insist on having a list of people they would receive? I mean, if would you have let them go, then of course they were even better off not receiving such a list, not to be in a position to have -- to make any counteroffer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not present personally, but what you heard was that it's the village of Berkovici, I think, when the civilians expressed their loyalty and they asked to go to territory that was under BiH Army control. I think towards Volo -- Olovo, but they didn't want to take them in as civilians probably because they stayed with the Serb side for a long time, and then they were returned to the detention unit -- no, the collection centre, in Rogatica. And then maybe later, in order to be able to go to their territory, they had to portray themselves as prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Save me what probably was the case. Tell us what you know. Then you would say they should be made prisoners of war to convince the other side that a 100-year-old lady was to be exchanged not to be a civilian but to be a prisoner of war? I'm just asking you whether you're serious in telling us that that explains the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't speak about that woman. I was speaking about the civilian population from Berkovici and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the list of elderly which was presented to you on which we find, among others, this old lady, three times: First in February; then in April; and, finally, reported to have deceased in August. I'm talking about that, not about anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the reason was, why they were --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, could you again repeat your answer because the interpreters couldn't catch you, your words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why they were treated as prisoners of war. Was it for an exchange maybe? But I claim with full responsibility that these elderly people were not in military remand prison. They were in the collection centre. That is really the only thing I can say in response to that question. I have nothing to add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, we've seen quite a list of persons. How many rooms were there for the civilians, and how many rooms were there for the military prisoners? Or prisoners of war, whatever you would ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean in Rasadnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I mean in Rasadnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I really didn't go in there. I don't know how big it is, how many rooms were used. I have -- didn't enter, so I cannot tell you about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you also have no personal knowledge about how they were separated, if they were separated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were separated. There was a detention facility and then there was the collection centre on the other side. I cannot say how many rooms belonged to which one. I did not go in there, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions on a totally different subject. Could you have a look at paragraph 12 of your statement. You have a hard copy with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have it here on paper. You don't have to look for it out there. You don't have to put it up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we'll do it anyhow, if you wouldn't mind. Could I ask you a few questions. First of all, you're talking about listening to Radio BiH of Sarajevo and reports sent to them by Fadil Heljic. Could you tell us what time-frame are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally did not listen to Radio BH Sarajevo. We had a person who was in charge who was a ham radio operator, and he gave us information about these intercepted communications of theirs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So where it says, "very often we would listen," the accurate statement is "very often a person I know would listen to Radio BiH?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, all right. Yes. A mistake was made there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore, you also didn't hear personally that it was reported that there were cases of euthanasia and cannibalism.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't hear it with my own ears, but I received information from a ham radio operator of ours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you know Fadil Heljic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew him before the war. He was a mailman at the post office in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you have any contact with him during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You tell us that Fadil Heljic received orders to bombard the public with these kind of statements. Could you tell us how you know that he received such orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we knew through their radio communications. I already mentioned this ham radio operator of ours who intercepted their communications, and he told us that orders were received from Sarajevo how this misinformation should be communicated in order to blacken the Serb side as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who was the ham radio operator who conveyed all this information to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Vukola Mandza. He was a good ham radio operator before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you received all of this information you're revealing here through him. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you also referred to a document - and I think that was one of the corrections, Mr. Ivetic, when I'm right - a document which shows that it was all lies. Could you explain this a bit more about this document because we do not know. What kind of a document is it? You say document so and so shows that these were lies and fabrication and then what -- what -- what document is it? Is it a letter? Is it an official document? Is it a newspaper article? What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a document that was sent to us by this Vukola Mandza. He intercepted radio communications and sent this document to us so that we would have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. But my question was what kind of a document it is. You now explained how you received, but could you tell us what it is, the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is a document where what is written in may statement is written. That is to say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you commented on that document, you drew certain conclusions from it, and since we have not -- we have not received that document, I'd like to know from you what that document is. What kind of a document is it. Is it a newspaper article? Is it an official report? Is it a combat report? A daily report? Is it a letter? What kind of a document is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, as far as I can remember, I saw this document when I testified in the case of President Radovan Karadzic. This document did exist in his case. I don't know whether it exists here, but that's the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, have you seen the document then after you testified in the case against Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It wasn't shown to you during the interview?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean the interview by the Mladic Defence when you were giving your statement. Was it then shown to you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can no longer understand or hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer. My question was whether the document was shown to you during your interview by the Mladic Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, again, my question: What kind of a document is it? Because you draw conclusions on the basis of that document; therefore, I would like to know what the document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can I correct the record, Your Honour, because you are incorrect that you have not received the document? You have received the document and you've given it an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I would have preferred, as a matter of fact, that it was referred to by the Exhibit number unless it was at a later stage that the exhibit number was given to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You gave the exhibit number today, Your Honours. It was tendered by myself as an associated exhibit to his statement with the number 1D3122. It received Exhibit D851, I believe -- 0.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are right, Mr. Ivetic, but it was not shown to us. It was just admitted. We didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And Your Honour said it was not received. If something is admitted into evidence, it is received by the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But that's not the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm glad to accept that after the change of the numbers that this is apparently then -- let's have a look at it. It may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One of the two associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, one of two. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the new number. Yes, paragraph 12. Yes. That must then be 1D03122, and that was the new number given. That all -- well, I'll have a look at it later. But I'd first like to know from you, Witness, what this document is. Apart from, I stand corrected, Mr. Ivetic, that we haven't received it. But what is the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think the witness has already answered that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, wait -- wait -- yes, he -- no, he has not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He has indeed. I can give you the transcript reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I'm not at this moment at this -- I -- if he has answered it, then he'll answer it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What is the document? I asked you -- gave you several options, newspaper article, anything else ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it's something different. It's not a newspaper article. This ham radio operator, when he intercepted that, he sent this document to us on a type-written page. It's like a dispatch or something that was sent to the command of the brigade. He didn't send us combat reports, I mean, the ham radio operator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do now understand that where the witness earlier testified how he received it, that it is also to be understood as a transcript of what was intercepted by the ham radio. That wasn't clear to me. It is clear to me now. Then could I have a look at it to see ... Could we have it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, before we further look at the document, you told us that you saw this document during the Karadzic trial because you said then the document was there. Now, when did you see it for the first time? Was it given to you by the ham radio operator, or did you see it for the first time in the Karadzic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had seen it before the Radovan Karadzic case. I saw it immediately. As soon as the ham radio operator intercepted this information, he immediately submitted it to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I -- could we move a little bit further up in the B/C/S version. Yes. And on the top, it says "Lelek." Do you know who did write that there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This thing up here in the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this was written by the Defence of Dr. Radovan Karadzic, that they had this document and that they wrote that that document should be submitted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you -- you said you received that right away. Did you keep a copy at the time or did you destroy it or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that single copy remained in the archives of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it known, Mr. Ivetic, I'm also looking at you, where this document was retrieved?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe the ERN range is from the Prosecution's collection of documents that they claim from the Drina Corps, but I have obviously did not get the document from the archives myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: I don't have that information to hand, Your Honours, but I can certainly check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please do that. Then I would like to have an opportunity to at least briefly read the document and see whether I have any further questions in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I suggest we take an early break --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that at least we can read what we had already received in evidence earlier today but which I had no opportunity to read yet. We'll take an early break and we'll see after the break whether I have any further questions for you in relation to this document. If, meanwhile, the Office of the Prosecutor could provide us with background information of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been told already by two colleagues it is from our Drina Corps collection. I can find further details, if you wish. Or I can try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think that's the most important information that it was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. And could I have a hard copy during the break so that can I read it. Witness, we'll take a break, 20 minutes. Mr. Ivetic, could you already give us an indication as to how much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I can complete in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In 15 minutes. Then -- You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 1.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom. Meanwhile, I have a few questions to the parties. Mr. Ivetic, the witness suggested that the word "Lelek" had been added during the Karadzic case. Therefore, the document as we see it before us then would not be the document which was retrieved from the Drina Corps. That's one. Therefore, I would like the Prosecution to verify whether it's exactly the same document or whether it's just the handwritten "Lelek" which is missing, and also whether it's the complete document, whether there is -- this is the one and only page of that document. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can provide some additional information. The document as uploaded in our e-court is the -- well, it is the document that was on the Karadzic -- that was in the Karadzic case as their number 1D06833. So I believe Your Honour is correct that the -- the -- this handwritten -- this one with the handwritten notation is from the Karadzic case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I do not know yet. It could have been there originally as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It could have. It could have as well. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore that is a conclusion which needs to be verified first and that's what I invited the Prosecution to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also whether it's the complete document. Witness, I have a few questions on the document which is now before us on the screen and which you commented in your statement, paragraph 12. Do I understand well that this document is a dispatch sent by the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade to the Drina Corps command to the Visegrad Tactical Group command and the Rudo Tactical Group command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is my understanding also correct that it reflects what a person who has intercepted a radio communication, what he reports to be the content of the conversation he intercepted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did you see that contemporaneously in 1992, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was it you who received it and instructed it to be sent to the corps command or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not receive this. This was the duty of the assistant chief of staff for intelligence and security. He was the one who received this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Was there any specific reason why you looked at this report in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the evening when we met up at the brigade command, the assistant chief of staff for security and intelligence gave all of us this document to peruse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this the whole of the document, or is it part of a document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't see if the document is complete because I don't see the bottom of the page. I don't know whether the sentence at the bottom of the page is, indeed, the last sentence of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question is whether you have any recollection whether it was, as it appears before us, a one-page document, or whether it was a more-page document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't remember how many pages there were, but I remember that we received the document from the assistant chief of staff for intelligence and security, and I remember the contents. And I don't remember whether there was just one page, half a page, more than one page, I don't know how the ham radio operator presented it. He sent it to us and then we sent it to the command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Any information relevant for this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There does appear to be a second page to this document. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is how it was -- how it was disclosed to the Defence in its -- I take it that it's -- whether it electronic disclosure or any way else, that this is the full document was disclosed to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: If Your Honour would just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Meanwhile, I'll continue with a few more questions. Witness, you commented on it and you said what is contained in this document is not true, if I understand you well. Let's first leave it to the 700 Chetniks killed. You say that is not true or couldn't be true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Nothing of the contents is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's -- let's take it step by step. I do understand that you said: "15 armoured vehicles destroyed cannot be true because we had no 15 armoured vehicles. We had only 1 personal carrier and two tanks at the time." Therefore that is also not true in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It continues to say that -- that a lady was captured, more than 90 years old. Do you have any comment on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My only comment is that this is nothing but blatant lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And how do you know that? Are you -- do you know who are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that we never ever captured a 90-year-old woman anywhere up there. There was no need for us to go after 90-year-old women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, then, I take it that what is described as her fate is also not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where it says that a woman who was 90-plus years old in Laze, not true. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It further says that two of the wounded combatants were burned. That is not true either? And it's described as having happened in the Podzeplje area.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say that because Podzeplje did border on our area. It is on an entirely different side in the direction of Han Pijesak. That was not in the area of responsibility of our brigade, so I can't say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that's far away from where your unit was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now you say this document demonstrates that what was broadcasted by Radio BiH of Sarajevo is not true, and you specifically refer to Fadil Heljic having received instructions that they should dig as many mounds as possible along the road used by humanitarian convoys and UNPROFOR and UNHCR which point to a large number of dead being buried every day. How does this document, which, as you say, contains no truth at all --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how would that demonstrate that other information, which is about Muslims deceased, how would this document explain that that is not true, that the reporting is not true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were several such documents. I don't know where you can find them. They're all false. We intercepted them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But now apart from whether information in communications between two persons turns out to be false, my question is: How that intercepted conversation would demonstrate what you say was wrongly broadcasted on the radio or was contradicting the instructions received by the person who was broadcasting that information, which is quite different from what is dealt with in this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll not repeat it. I leave it to the parties to argue on this matter. I have a final few questions. Were you aware of 55 Chetniks, as it is written here, released from prison but they considered -- the interlocutors considered that to be a mistake. Are you aware of 55 Chetniks, as they call the persons, to be released from prison by apparently the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were never 55 Chetniks or what they call Chetniks and I would call them our fighters. In any case, there were never 55 of them captured them in Zepa at all, so this is yet another lie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean not 55 of your fighters, or never 55 at all in Zepa, or in Muslim hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know only know that at the beginning of the war, the very beginning, 45 were killed. They were members of the VRS on the way to our -- to the repeater where our crew as, and as they were crossing Budicin brook --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Killing of 45 persons, which is serious, is, however, something different from what my question was about; that is, about 55 people being detained, captured. Therefore, I repeat my question: If you say, never 55 of them were captured, do you mean just in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not from our brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot claim that if they were captured they were not from other brigades.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say it's still possible from other brigades, 55 persons were captured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I'm talking about our brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you tell us where in this document it says that the information relates to your brigade only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't say so. However, I know what the situation was with our brigade, and I know what information would pertain to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that you were aware of that. Now, has it ever crossed your mind that the conversation which was intercepted may have dealt with a far broader theatre than your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I said that I did not work on this document. It was the assistant chief of staff for intelligence and security who worked on this document. I only read it at a meeting. This was not a part of my duties. It was the assistant chief of staff who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear to me. Nevertheless, you draw all kind of conclusions off the basis of this document, and I'm focusing on that. If you say, We had no 15 armoured vehicles, therefore, it must be a lie that they were destroyed, then that assumes or presumes that these were 15 armoured vehicles of your brigade. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a lie that there were that many armoured vehicles. It's a lie. I did not have that many of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't have them, but as with the 55 prisoners, they may have destroyed 15 armoured vehicles elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my view, this is nothing but a lie. When it comes to the number of soldiers who were killed, the number of tanks that were destroyed, everything false. And now why Dr. Becir Heljic wrote that, he was from Zepa but lived in Sarajevo. What he said and what Fadil had conveyed, I don't know why they did that. You should ask them. You should talk to them, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness, I asked you about the fate of two wounded combatants in the Podzeplje area. You said you wouldn't know because that was far away from where your unit was. Have you ever considered that the information in this intercept may have covered areas far away from your unit? Whether false or true, it's a different matter, but that it was not limited to the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I don't know whether the brigade commander with his assistant for security and intelligence discussed this ever at all. As far as I'm concerned, I never discussed this document with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, at least with the Karadzic Defence and with the Mladic Defence, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And your question is what? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you said I never discussed it with anyone; but I said but you did discuss it with the Karadzic and the Mladic Defence. True?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but never before. I thought that you were asking me about the time when that happened, whether I spoke about this document with somebody in the brigade. No, I did not. It was only the brigade commander and his assistant for intelligence and security who could probably discuss this document, not me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have no further questions on this document, but Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. MacDonald, I think we -- you have concluded your cross-examination. I had some questions. Mr. Ivetic is now, I think it's his turn. If you want to provide us information, then that's appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I understand this document was not disclosed individually but as part of the EDS system; I mean, the entire document is on there. I think the reason there's only one page is that that is what was taken in the Karadzic case. The translation request I think was from the Defence in that case, and they only requested the first page be translated. I understand, and I don't claim to speak B/C/S, but the second -- this second page I have seems to follow on and be in the same typeset and so forth and so on. That is the information I have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is there any sender visible?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It appears to be type signed Commander Captain Rajko Kusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in -- in -- in view of the answers I have received to my questions, I -- perhaps it always is better to have a complete document. Whatever appears on the second page, unless there are surprising matters, I would not be primarily interested in it, but perhaps the parties could have a look at and see whether it adds anything to what can we discussed until now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We'll do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Judge Fluegge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lelek, also with respect to paragraph 12 of your statement, there you say: "Fadil Heljic received orders to bombarded the public with such statements directly from Sarajevo from his relative, Dr. Becir Heljic." I just want to know what is the basis of this statement, the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The objective was to create a bad image of Serbs as aggressors and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that the Muslim side should be portrayed as those who were suffering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, this is not my question. I would like to know the basis of your knowledge about such an instruction by Dr. Becir Heljic. How do you know that, that he instructed his relative in that way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The ham radio operator who was always intercepting their conversations knew that Becir Heljic was sending all of these messages to Fadil Heljic in Zepa because Becir Heljic hailed from Zepa and lived in Zepa before the war. He was a doctor when the war started. He left and settled in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You received this information from the ham radio operator, and you -- earlier you gave his name. Was that -- did he tell you orally, you personally, or was it information given to the brigade or to the commander? In which way did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've told you once he did not give me that information personally. He typed up a dispatch and sent it to the brigade commander. He didn't really speak to anybody about that. His communication was written and sent to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I also have one short follow-up question which only came to my mind now. The person portrayed in this intercept is a doctor. Is it your evidence that that doctor must be Dr. Becir Heljic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I claim that it was Dr. Becir Heljic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what's the basis for that claim? Because in the intercept we only see that there is a doctor in Sarajevo, and there may be many doctors in Sarajevo. Do you have -- what's -- what is it that makes you claim that it is Dr. Heljic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not the only conversation that was intercepted. There were many such conversations where Dr. Becir Heljic's name was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any such -- now I have -- my last question, is you say, well, this was all false information to give a bad picture of the Serbs. If I read all this, then it mainly and primarily glorifies the Muslims being so successful in their actions and only on two points saying that the Serbs misbehaved. And you say it's false, all, anyhow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that this is all nothing but lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I -- I leave it to the parties to further argue on how compelling conclusions, how these documents should be -- this document should be interpreted against the background of what we know now, that is, that the witness did not himself listen to the BH radio because I don't think it would be of any use at this moment to further -- but if any of the parties has questions for the question of course feel free to ask them. Mr. Ivetic, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And first, I don't know whether Judge Fluegge is finished. He asked about the name of the operator, that is at temporary transcript page 65, line 21 through 22.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Thank you. Then I can continue with this document, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document identifies that this is a participant from Zepa and a doctor from Sarajevo. You've already told us about your understanding of who the doctor in Sarajevo is. Do you have any information as to who the participate in Zepa would have been?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Is that a question for me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, from Zepa, it was Heljic, the mailman, whatever. Fadil, Fadil. He's one. And the other one is Dr. Becir.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to move to another topic. At temporary transcript page 19, lines 12 through 22, and then at several points during the cross-examination, you repeatedly referenced a telegram or dispatch sent on the 23rd of May, 1992, which you said had been -- showed that you were not yet part of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to call up Prosecution Exhibit P00166 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, what we have on the screen is dated the 23rd of May, 1992. And I'd like to ask you, sir, if this might perhaps be the document that you kept referencing during the cross-examination of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if you could help us out, the Sokolac TO commander, what entity was that during the relevant time-period?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: That was this Territorial Defence in Sokolac and the Territorial Defence of Rogatica. But the one at Sokolac was higher ranking compared to Rogatica. That's why these dispatches were sent to them, because there were no links yet with the corps or the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you: You testified about not including the references to Uzamnica and the JNA depot there at Uzamnica. Do you recall when weapons were sent from Rogatica to Uzamnica?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I worked in the Territorial Defence Staff until 1990. And until then, that was not the case. It was probably the end of 1990 or the beginning of 1991. It was probably 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge of the reason why the TO weapons were sent to the JNA depot at Uzamnica near Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. MacDonald.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I think -- I think my friend is going to territory that was not covered in cross-examination. I spoke about simply mentioning something left out of the statement. Even the substance of that, I think we're straying away from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the same time, Mr. MacDonald, there was, of course, a suggestion in your later questioning that these were relevant and important matters and for that reason Mr. Ivetic is allowed to briefly go to the substance as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you have knowledge of the reason why the weapons of the TO were sent to the JNA depot at Uzamnica near Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: It was for security reasons. There were already these party divisions, and it's not only from our brigade that weapons went -- no, sorry, not brigades. Territorial Defence staffs. All the weapons were withdrawn into the depot, so no Territorial Defence staffs had weapons. This was done for the sake of safety and security, because these party divisions started already after the first multi-party elections were held.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to look at 65 ter number 31403.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Which I'm not sure if that received a P number. It was used but I don't know if it was tendered. I only have the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is the Official Note of the MUP interview, and I'd like to ask you: First of all, did the police officials that were interviewing you, did they record your interview to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: Well, I really wanted to explain this even before but I wasn't allowed to. This conversation took perhaps only five minutes. This official who worked at the MUP in this little notepad he just jotted things down: Do you know anything about the staffs? No. The Crisis Staffs? No. Did you enter, did you know anything about Rasadnik and these collection centres, and I said I heard that there was that at Borike but I never entered. That was it, five or six minutes. That was that. He left. I never received a statement from -- for me to sign. And there's also other incorrect information here. Over here, in this second paragraph, from the top --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you direct us to the other incorrect information in this Official Note from the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, other incorrect -- incorrect information, I would like to hear about that because it -- although it's not tendered, if I understand you well, the issue was whether the witness at the time said that he never entered the centres, whereas he now says that the -- we have dealt with that in quite some detail. Now the witness has repeatedly confirmed that he told those MUP officers that he did not enter the premises there, so in that respect at least the report seems to be confirmed. Now if there is other information which is incorrect, again it's not tendered so we wouldn't -- we wouldn't have it. We would not even be able to rely on it. Then if you consider that important and relevant, of course, you have an opportunity -- well, we come close to whether it still is something that was dealt with in cross-examination because that was focused exclusively on that one matter. But if you have some few short questions on that. But then of course we would have a look at the whole of the document, and then it should be tendered. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's a very short point that twice the witness tried to raise in cross-examination and Your Honour stopped him from answering it. So I think it does arise from it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- because you first did not know what he was going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, sometimes I stop witnesses because they are going beyond what is asked. But if you -- in that respect -- but again, if there is anything at this moment you would like to briefly address, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I could be very focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The end of the second paragraph of this Official Note, sir, that records the time-period you were chief of staff, is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we see the end of the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, that was a question and I was hoping you could answer, and I think it's what you wanted to raise. The second paragraph, is the date -- the dates that you are recorded, according to the MUP, as having been chief of staff, are they accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: They're not correct. I said to the MUP employee then that I was the chief in the brigade, the chief in the brigade, end of 1993 beginning of 1994, and that until the end of the war I was there, until Dayton. And what is written here is that I was appointed chief of staff of the Rogatica Brigade from the 4th of April, 1992, to the 21st of June, 1996. That's not correct at all. I was with my parents in the village there, and I was still involved with the village guards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I see that there's also a translation issue. Well, a transcription issue rather than a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you elicit from the witness when he was performing the function you consider we should know about, then it's -- will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yeah, why don't we just do it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell us what dates, as recall them, you served as chief of staff of the Rogatica Brigade, the correct dates?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I cannot give the exact dates, but I know it was the beginning -- the end of 1993, December 1993. Or even the beginning of 1994. January 1994. Not what is written here from the 4th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you were asked about the Rasadnik facility, and I'd like to ask you to assume that none of us have been to Rasadnik. How many buildings comprised the Rasadnik reception centre and the Rasadnik military remand prison?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: It consisted of two buildings. But this one here, the reception centre, it was longer and bigger than the one that was the military remand prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned loyal Muslim villages and your description of why they left Rogatica. Do you know what they did with the keys to their houses and the houses themselves prior to leaving?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I don't know what they did with them. Often they would even blow up their houses. They would plant these mines there, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could we ask -- Could you give us two or three names of persons who mined their houses and that were then -- that then did explode?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just know that Asonja [phoen], I can't remember the exact name, he wanted to enter the house and he came across a booby-trap and was killed in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was do you know specifically about mining, who did it, what houses, what families did so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say specifically because I personally did not see that, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you happen to know the village where that occurred, as my question dealt with the loyal Muslim villages that you had identified earlier in your examination?

utterances.speaker: MILOVAN LELEK
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the break I think I'm -- I've completely exhausted all my questions, so I think we can -- unless anyone else has any questions, I'm done with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. Macdonald, is that how I have to understand your nodding in a horizontal movement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACDONALD
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Since the Bench has no further questions, Mr. Lelek, this concludes your testimony. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague - a long way - and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn and we will resume Thursday, the 11th of December, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
